headline: KDE Connect is a free open source app that does everything better than Microsoft Phone Link
summary: This cross-platform app syncs notifications, shares clipboards, transfers files, and even turns your phone into a remote control, all without requiring an online account.
details: A new open source app, KDE Connect, is emerging as a superior alternative to Microsoft Phone Link for bridging Android and Windows devices. It offers a comprehensive suite of features including notification syncing, clipboard sharing, and robust file transfer capabilities.

Unlike Microsoft Phone Link, KDE Connect does not require users to create an online account, simplifying setup and enhancing privacy. It allows for seamless connection of multiple phones to a Windows app and vice versa, with broad cross-platform compatibility across Android, Windows, iOS, macOS, and Linux.

Setting up KDE Connect involves installing the app on desired devices, connecting them to the same Wi-Fi network, and linking them through the app. While it requires permissions for file access, notifications, and clipboard, its functionality is extensive.

Key features include real-time notification syncing and replying directly from your laptop, and shared clipboard functionality for effortless text transfer between devices. File sharing is also streamlined, making dedicated apps like Quick Share redundant for many users.

KDE Connect also offers advanced features like remote input, allowing your Android phone to function as a mouse, keyboard, or multimedia controller for your laptop. Users can also disable unused plugins to optimize battery life.

However, KDE Connect has a steeper learning curve than Microsoft Phone Link and its user interface may appear out of place on Windows compared to native apps. Its reliance on a local Wi-Fi network can also be a limitation when traveling, though a mobile hotspot can serve as a workaround.

Despite these minor drawbacks, the continuous development and responsiveness to user feedback inherent in open source projects make KDE Connect a compelling and powerful tool for enhancing productivity between Android and PC setups.

headline_marked: [[New Cars Share Data]] With Third Parties, Study Finds
headline: New Cars Share Data With Third Parties, Study Finds
summary: A study revealed that many new vehicles and their apps transmit sensitive information like VINs and precise locations to advertising and analytics companies.
details: A recent study from Northeastern University analyzed 21 late-model cars and 30 automaker apps, finding that 19 of the vehicles sent data to at least one third-party company via Wi-Fi. Seven of the apps were found to be passing identifiers such as VINs, email addresses, and precise locations to advertising and analytics firms.

General Motors' apps were particularly implicated, with myCadillac, myChevrolet, myBuick, and myGMC apps sending VINs to 10 companies, including Microsoft and Adobe. This is despite GM being under an FTC privacy order since January, which restricts the sale of driver data and requires express consent for data collection and sharing.

HondaLink was found to send VINs and location data to Amplitude, while the Lincoln and MyNISSAN apps also shared identifiers. Unlike a phone's advertising ID, a VIN cannot be reset, allowing ad companies to link a car owner's identity to their online activities.

While 10 of the tested cars did not contact advertising or tracking domains on their own, their associated apps often did. For instance, the Buick Envista's app exposed owners to 23 ad and tracking companies, and the Nissan Ariya's to 25.

Most of the tested apps contacted at least one advertising or analytics company. The researchers noted that the actual data sharing could be higher, as they could only capture cellular data for one vehicle and could not decrypt internal vehicle traffic.

Manufacturers largely stated that the data flows align with their vendor contracts, with some attributing tracking to web pages within their apps or placing responsibility on the owner to accept terms for third-party services. Privacy policies often disclosed potential data sharing without specifying recipients or reasons.

Honda has reportedly taken steps to address the issue, asking Amplitude to delete location data and updating HondaLink to cease sending it. However, other manufacturers indicated that disabling data collection could lead to reduced functionality or disable key features like navigation and over-the-air updates.
